John / team — attaching the requested artifacts (see attachments list below). Summary narrative follows; full details in the attached PDF and SVG diagram.

High-level summary (short):
- Deployment modes: Redwood supports Hosted, Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Private (customer VPC + private control plane). For Private, the control plane is logically separated and can be run in our managed control plane (customer VPC peering) or a customer-managed control plane inside their VPC (recommended for regulated workloads).
- Control plane vs Data plane: control plane handles model routing, orchestration, and metadata; it sits in a different network domain and communicates to data plane nodes over authenticated mTLS channels. Data plane (inference workers) processes customer requests and never stores customer model artifacts in cleartext outside ephemeral GPU-local storage.
- Tenant isolation: enforced via a multi-layer strategy:
  * Network: per-tenant subnets/VLANs and security groups; egress-only NATs for outbound telemetry flows when required.
  * Compute: tenant-assigned GPU pools with cgroup isolation and job-level scheduling. Dedicated customer pools are pinned to physical hosts to reduce noisy neighbor risk.
  * Process/Namespace: container namespaces and strict RBAC at the orchestration layer; KV cache encryption-at-rest.
- KMS / HSM: we support customer-managed keys (CMKs) via cloud KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and on-prem HSMs through an AMQP-based gateway. Keys for tenant encryption and signing are stored as sealed references in the control plane; key material never resides on inference worker disk. Key usage auditing is available and can be exported as part of an evidence pack (we can include KMS access logs for a short time window upon request).
- Egress & routing policy: by default Private deploys restrict egress to whitelisted destinations (customer telemetry collectors, patch repos). Inter-VPC communication is via peering or transit gateway with ACLs at the subnet edge.

SIG / CAIQ pointers (short):
- We maintain a living CAIQ crosswalk in Drive (link below) with pointers to where each control is addressed in our SOC2 pack and architecture docs.
- For SIG, our recommended packet includes: network diagram (annotated), segregation matrix (CSV), sample KMS audit slice (redacted), and the SOC2 assertion summary.

Attachments included in this email:
- private-deploy-topology-v1.png (annotated network topology, 1200x800)
- kms-boundary-annotated.pdf (HSM/KMS options, custody flow, sample audit query)
- segregation-matrix.csv (mapping of isolation controls to SIG/SOC2 families)

Quick ASCII topology (for inline reference):

  [Customer VPC]                                  [Redwood Control Plane]
  +----------------------+         peering       +--------------------------+
  |  Subnet-A (Workers)  | <--------------------> |  Control Plane (mTLS/API) |
  |  - GPU hosts (pinned)|                        |  - Orchestration          |
  |  - Tenant VLANs      |                        |  - Key reference store    |
  +----------------------+                        +--------------------------+
          |                                         ^          |
          |                                         |          |
     Egress ACLs  ---> [Transit GW / NAT] ----->  Logging    KMS proxy
          |                                                     |
          v                                                     v
       Customer SIEM                                         Cloud KMS / HSM

Notes on evidence extracts:
- We can produce a KMS-call audit slice (ISO timestamps) and a short network ACL export for the subnets used in your deployment.
- For SOC2 reviewers we typically provide the annotated diagram + segregation matrix + sample logs (redacted).

Next steps: Lauren, Dev and I will stitch the Drive folder and HubSpot record. John, if you can confirm the scope (full SIG vs just network + KMS) we'll prioritize artifacts.

—Kim
